# ATHENA: Voice System Improvement Review & Implementation Blueprint

(Research completed) (18 November 2026) (Zero-cost, local-first)

## 1. Executive recommendation

Athena has a functioning text conversation loop\:

- HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend.
- FastAPI backend.
- Ollama serving `athena-llama:3b`\.
- SQLite conversation history.

What it does not have is a voice system. There is currently no microphone capture, speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio transport, or turn-taking logic.

The next development phase should therefore be **Athena Voice v0.1**, not another round of text-model optimisation.

My recommendation is to build a deliberately simple, mostly local voice loop\:

1. User clicks a microphone button.
2. Browser records one utterance.
3. Local speech recognition converts the recording to text.
4. User reviews the transcript.
5. Existing Ollama chat endpoint generates a response.
6. Athena displays the response and speaks it.
7. User can stop playback at any time.

Start with push-to-talk. Do not begin with an always-listening assistant, wake-word detection, continuous streaming, or autonomous interruption handling.

**Recommended first implementation**

**Browser microphone capture**

MediaRecorder, initiated only by the user

---

**whisper.cpp**

Local CPU transcription, initially using base.en

---

**Existing Ollama model**

Keep Athena's current intelligence layer intact

---

**Browser speechSynthesis**

First speech output, with Piper as the local neural TTS upgrade

This is the best balance between getting a working voice experience quickly and preserving the local-first direction.

The important distinction: **the first version should prove the interaction loop, not perfect the voice.**

---

## 2. The architecture Athena needs

The architecture should keep speech recognition, language generation, and speech synthesis independent. That allows us to replace one component without rebuilding the application.

### Proposed data flow

```mermaid

flowchart TD
    A["User clicks microphone"] --> B["Browser microphone permission"]
    B --> C["MediaRecorder captures audio"]
    C --> D["POST /api/transcribe"]
    D --> E["Temporary audio file"]
    E --> F["Audio conversion: 16 kHz mono WAV"]
    F --> G["STT adapter: whisper.cpp"]
    G --> H["Transcript returned to browser"]
    H --> I["User reviews / edits transcript"]
    I --> J["POST /api/chat"]
    J --> K["FastAPI conversation service"]
    K --> L["Ollama: athena-llama:3b"]
    K <--> M[("SQLite history")]
    L --> N["Completed response"]
    N --> O["Display response"]
    N --> P["TTS adapter"]
    P --> Q["Browser speechSynthesis initially"]
    P -. "Later replacement" .-> R["Local Piper TTS"]
    Q --> S["Audio playback"]
    R --> S
    S --> T["Stop / interrupt control"]
```

### What changes, and what stays

| Component | Decision |
|--------|--------|
| FastAPI | Keep |
| Ollama | Keep |
| `athena-llama:3b` | Keep initially |
| SQLite | Keep |
| Existing text chat | Preserve as fallback |
| Microphone capture | Add |
| STT | Add as replaceable provider |
| TTS | Add as replaceable provider |
| Audio storage | Temporary only, unless explicitly enabled later |
| Streaming | Defer until basic voice loop works |

I would introduce only two small provider boundaries initially\:

- `transcribe_audio(audio_file)` for speech recognition.
- `synthesize_speech(text)` for speech generation.

The application should not care whether those functions are implemented by Whisper, Vosk, Piper, or another engine.

That is enough abstraction. We do not need an agent framework or a large plugin architecture.

---

## 3. Speech-to-text options

There are four realistic candidates worth considering.

### STT comparison

| Option | Local/offline | Resource profile | Integration | Assessment |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Browser Web Speech Recognition | Not guaranteed | Browser-managed | Very easy | Temporary experiment |
| whisper.cpp | Yes | Base model: about 388 MB runtime reference | Moderate | **Recommended** |
| faster-whisper | Yes | Small INT8 benchmark: about 1.48 GB RAM | Easy Python API | Secondary candidate |
| Vosk | Yes | Small models: about 300 MB runtime | Easy Python API | Lightweight fallback |

#### A. Browser Web Speech Recognition

(Fastest prototype, privacy caveat)

The browser's Web Speech API exposes speech recognition through `SpeechRecognition`\.

Advantages\:

- Very little application code.
- No separate model installation.
- Results can arrive incrementally.
- Easy to test whether the microphone and conversation experience feel natural.

The problem is privacy and browser support.

MDN explicitly warns that some browsers use a server-based recognition engine by default, meaning audio is sent to a web service. On-device recognition is possible through `processLocally`, but requires browser support and installed language packs. The API is also not universally supported.  [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Verdict\:** useful for a quick disposable experiment. Do not make it Athena's default STT system.

It is particularly unsuitable for private conversations about coursework, personal matters, or sensitive documents unless the processing location is known and accepted.

#### B. whisper.cpp

(Recommended STT)

Repository: [ggml-org/whisper.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp)

This is a C/C++ implementation of OpenAI Whisper, with CPU-only inference, integer quantisation, and Windows support through MSVC or MinGW. It is released under the MIT licence.  [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Its main advantage here is that it avoids introducing a large PyTorch runtime into Athena's existing Python environment.

The upstream project publishes these approximate memory figures\:

| Model | Disk | Runtime memory |
|--------|--------|--------|
| tiny | 75 MiB | \~273 MB |
| base | 142 MiB | \~388 MB |
| small | 466 MiB | \~852 MB |
| medium | 1.5 GiB | \~2.1 GB |
| large | 2.9 GiB | \~3.9 GB |

These are upstream reference figures, not measurements from your laptop. The `base.en` model should be benchmarked directly rather than assuming its exact memory footprint from the generic base entry.  [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp/blob/master/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**My starting choice: `base.en`\.**

Why?

- It is an English-only model.
- OpenAI's model documentation says English-only variants tend to perform better for English applications, particularly at tiny and base sizes.
- It is substantially smaller than the larger model families.
- It does not require a Python machine-learning framework to run the transcription engine.  [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

If accuracy is insufficient, test `small.en` next. Do not begin with medium or large.

One implementation detail matters: the current `whisper-cli` example expects 16-bit WAV audio. Its documentation demonstrates converting audio to 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM with FFmpeg.  [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

That means our first local pipeline will need\:

```text
Browser recording
    ↓
Temporary WebM/Opus file
    ↓
FFmpeg conversion
    ↓
16 kHz mono PCM WAV
    ↓
whisper-cli.exe
    ↓
Transcript
```

`MediaRecorder` supports different recording containers and codecs depending on the browser. We should inspect supported MIME types instead of hardcoding one format.  [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaRecorder?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaRecorder?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

#### C. faster-whisper

Repository: [SYSTRAN/faster-whisper](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper)

This reimplements Whisper using CTranslate2 and supports CPU INT8 inference.

It is attractive because\:

- It has a Python API.
- It supports CPU execution.
- Its audio decoding uses PyAV, so a system FFmpeg installation is not required.
- Its documentation reports lower memory consumption than the original OpenAI Whisper implementation in its tested configurations.  [GitHub](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

However, the published small-model CPU benchmark is important.

For a 13-minute recording, the project reports\:

| Implementation | RAM usage | Processing time |
|--------|--------|--------|
| whisper.cpp, FP32 | 1,049 MB | 2m05s |
| faster-whisper, FP32 | 2,257 MB | 2m37s |
| faster-whisper, INT8 | 1,477 MB | 1m42s |

Those measurements were taken on an Intel Core i7-12700K with eight threads, not your Ryzen 5 5625U. They should not be treated as expected Athena performance.  [GitHub](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The project declares Python 3.9 or greater, but that does not by itself guarantee that every dependency has a compatible Windows wheel for Python 3.13. We would need to test the installation.

**Verdict\:** worth keeping as an alternative if the Python integration advantage becomes important. Not my first choice for an 8 GB machine.

#### D. Vosk

Website: [Vosk](https://alphacephei.com/vosk/)

Vosk is an offline speech-recognition toolkit with a streaming API.

Its small models typically require around 300 MB of runtime memory. The published small US English model is approximately 40 MB on disk.  [alphacephei.com](https://alphacephei.com/vosk/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [alphacephei.com](https://alphacephei.com/vosk/models?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Advantages\:

- Low resource requirements.
- Offline operation.
- Straightforward Python installation.
- Streaming recognition.
- Vocabulary adaptation.

Limitations\:

- The listed lightweight English model is US English.
- Its reported accuracy figures are based on datasets such as LibriSpeech and TED-LIUM, not Ghanaian English.
- Its small model may be less accurate than Whisper for varied conversational speech and technical vocabulary.

**Verdict\:** the fallback if Whisper proves too slow or difficult to build.

### STT decision

I would not install every candidate.

Start with\:

1. `whisper.cpp`
2. `base.en`
3. CPU inference
4. Four threads initially
5. Benchmark actual recordings

Only consider Vosk if Whisper's speed or memory behaviour is unacceptable.

---

## 4. Text-to-speech options

Speech output is equally important. Athena needs a recognisable voice, not merely a computer reading text aloud.

### TTS comparison

| Option | Local/offline | Voice quality | Resource/integration | Verdict |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Browser speechSynthesis | Depends on installed voice engine | Varies by Windows voice | Very low friction | Start here |
| Piper | Yes | Neural, generally suitable for conversational speech | Lightweight-oriented ONNX engine | **Local target** |
| Kokoro | Yes | Promising, more expressive candidate | 82M parameters plus Python/Torch stack | Test later |

#### A. Browser speechSynthesis

[MDN SpeechSynthesis documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechSynthesis)

This is the quickest way to make Athena speak.

The API can\:

- Retrieve available voices.
- Select a voice.
- Speak text.
- Pause and resume.
- Cancel queued speech.

It is widely supported across browsers.  [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechSynthesis?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The biggest advantage is that we do not need another neural model running alongside Ollama.

The limitation is that voice availability and quality depend on the browser and underlying operating-system speech engine. We must inspect the actual voices installed on Windows and test them.

Also, do not automatically assume that every platform voice is offline. We should test speech output with the network disconnected.

**Verdict\:** use it for Milestone 3. It gets us from text-only to audible conversation without introducing another model dependency.

#### B. Piper

Repository: [OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl)

Piper is a local neural TTS engine using VITS voices exported to ONNX Runtime. Its Python API supports WAV synthesis and provides a generator-based synthesis interface.  [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/VOICES.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/API_PYTHON.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

English voices are available in\:

- British English (`en_GB`\)
- US English (`en_US`\)

There is no listed Twi voice.  [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/VOICES.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Piper is a strong candidate for Athena's eventual local voice because\:

- It runs locally.
- It is designed for CPU-oriented use.
- It has a Python API.
- It supports synthesis in chunks.
- It can be integrated behind a simple TTS adapter.

There are two things to be aware of.

**First, Windows installation.** Piper's C/C++ documentation explicitly describes a Windows CMake build and installation of its CLI and runtime DLLs. Its Python API documentation gives a straightforward `pip install piper-tts` route, but does not establish that the exact Python 3.13 environment here will install cleanly. We should test it in an isolated environment before changing Athena's dependencies.  [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/libpiper/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/API_PYTHON.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Second, licensing.** The current engine is GPL-3.0-or-later, but the voice models have separate licensing conditions. Piper specifically warns that some common Lessac-derived voices have restrictive licensing, including restrictions on commercial use. The model card and the full training lineage need to be checked for the exact voice selected.  [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/LICENSING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/LICENSING.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The project is also actively seeking maintainers, so maintenance continuity should be monitored rather than assumed.  [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Verdict\:** my preferred local neural TTS candidate, subject to a Windows installation and voice-licence check.

#### C. Kokoro

Repository: [hexgrad/kokoro](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro)

Kokoro is an 82-million-parameter open-weight TTS model. Its project publishes Apache-licensed weights and examples for American and British English voices.  [GitHub](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

It is worth knowing about because its voice quality is promising.

However, the Python pipeline uses PyTorch and other components, including `misaki` and `espeak-ng`\. The 82-million-parameter figure alone does not tell us the complete runtime memory footprint. No benchmark in the reviewed documentation establishes its performance on this exact Ryzen laptop.

It also has no listed Twi support.  [GitHub](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Verdict\:** a later voice-quality experiment, not a first implementation dependency.

### TTS decision

Use browser `speechSynthesis` first. Once Athena can complete spoken conversations, replace it with Piper if the browser voice is inadequate or fails the offline test.

This is a deliberate decision to avoid loading another machine-learning runtime before we have measured the first complete voice loop.

---

## 5. Recommended stacks

There are three useful levels of implementation.

**Stack A: Fastest disposable demonstration**

(Not privacy-guaranteed)

- Browser SpeechRecognition
- Browser speechSynthesis
- Existing FastAPI and Ollama

This is the fastest way to test the interaction experience. It is not suitable as Athena's permanent local-first speech system because recognition may use a remote service.

---

**Stack B: Recommended Athena MVP**

(Build this first)

- Browser `getUserMedia` \+ `MediaRecorder`
- Local `whisper.cpp` using `base.en`
- FFmpeg for audio conversion
- Existing FastAPI + Ollama
- Browser `speechSynthesis`
- SQLite conversation history

This gives us local speech recognition and keeps the initial TTS dependency simple.

---

**Stack C: Fully local voice target**

(Target after MVP works)

- Browser microphone capture
- Local `whisper.cpp`
- Local Ollama
- Local Piper TTS
- No external speech-processing service

This is the intended long-term architecture for the first genuinely local voice version.

**Fallback for STT\:** Vosk's small English model.

**Fallback for TTS\:** browser speechSynthesis until Piper is successfully installed and tested.

---

## 6. The machine's resource budget

Your machine is capable of running this architecture, but memory management matters.

Known facts\:

- Ryzen 5 5625U, 6 cores / 12 threads.
- Approximately 8 GB RAM.
- Integrated Radeon graphics.
- No verified CUDA-capable GPU.
- Ollama reports approximately 2.3 GB for the loaded `athena-llama:3b` configuration at 2,048 context.

The reported Ollama figure is not a complete measurement of total Windows memory consumption.

### Practical resource strategy

| Component | Initial approach |
|--------|--------|
| Ollama | Keep the existing 3B model |
| STT | `whisper.cpp` base.en |
| STT process | Load for transcription, then exit |
| TTS | Use browser system voice initially |
| Audio | Temporary files, deleted after transcription |
| Threads | Start with 4 for Whisper |
| Inference | Sequential, not simultaneous |
| Larger models | Do not introduce yet |

The important distinction is that the system should not try to transcribe, generate a long response, and synthesise speech simultaneously.

The intended sequence is\:

```text
Record audio
    ↓
Stop microphone
    ↓
Transcribe
    ↓
Release STT process
    ↓
Generate response with Ollama
    ↓
Speak response
```

The `whisper.cpp` base model's published runtime memory estimate is around 388 MB. This is far more attractive for this machine than running a small faster-whisper model with its published INT8 benchmark of approximately 1.48 GB.  [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp/blob/master/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

I would initially leave Ollama's model residency alone. If memory pressure becomes severe, we can test unloading it between stages. Ollama supports `keep_alive: 0` to unload a model immediately, but that introduces model reload latency on the next request.  [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Do not implement an unload/reload mechanism before measuring actual memory pressure.

---

## 7. Voice interaction design

This is where Athena starts becoming a companion rather than a chat page.

### The initial interaction state machine

```mermaid

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> RequestingPermission: Click microphone
    RequestingPermission --> Recording: Permission granted
    RequestingPermission --> Error: Permission denied
    Recording --> Transcribing: Stop recording
    Recording --> Error: Recording failure
    Transcribing --> ReviewTranscript: Transcript returned
    Transcribing --> Error: STT failure
    ReviewTranscript --> Thinking: Confirm / Send
    Thinking --> Speaking: Response received
    Thinking --> Idle: Text response only
    Speaking --> Idle: Playback complete
    Speaking --> Idle: Stop speaking
    Speaking --> Recording: Manual interrupt
    Error --> Idle: Retry / Dismiss
```

### Interface requirements

The interface should visibly distinguish these states\:

| State | What Athena displays |
|--------|--------|
| Idle | Ready |
| Requesting permission | Requesting microphone access |
| Recording | Listening |
| Transcribing | Processing speech |
| Review transcript | Recognised words |
| Thinking | Athena is thinking |
| Speaking | Athena is speaking |
| Error | What failed and how to retry |

The first version should include\:

- A microphone button.
- A visible recording indicator.
- A transcript display that the user can edit.
- A Send/Confirm action.
- A Stop Speaking button.
- A text input fallback.
- A clear error message.

Microphone access through `getUserMedia()` requires permission and a secure context. A localhost application is an appropriate development context. The browser also provides microphone-use indicators.  [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getUserMedia...?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getUserMedia...?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

### Preventing Athena from hearing herself

For the initial version, this is straightforward\:

- Stop microphone recording before transcription.
- Do not listen while Athena is speaking.
- Do not restart the microphone automatically after TTS.
- Require a fresh user action to begin another recording.

This avoids the feedback loop where Athena's own speech becomes the next user transcript.

For later hands-free interaction, we will need voice activity detection and acoustic echo cancellation. The browser supports audio constraints such as echo cancellation, but they should not be treated as a guarantee that self-transcription will disappear.

### Push-to-talk versus hands-free

Push-to-talk should be the first implementation.

Hands-free interaction requires decisions about\:

- When the user has finished speaking.
- How long a pause is allowed.
- Whether a pause means the user is thinking or has finished.
- Whether the assistant should interrupt.
- How to distinguish the assistant's speaker output from the user's voice.

Those are interaction-design problems as much as technical problems. We should observe real usage before solving them.

---

## 8. Implementation roadmap

The sequence below is intentionally small. Every milestone has a test and an acceptance criterion.

### Milestone 0: Verify text-response completeness

(P0 — Before voice integration)

The previous response terminated mid-sentence. `num_predict=500` is a plausible cause, but we have not verified it.

Ollama's chat API returns useful metadata\:

- `done`
- `done_reason`
- `total_duration`
- `load_duration`
- `prompt_eval_count`
- `eval_count`
- `eval_duration`

These are documented fields in the current API.  [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Files likely to change**

- `app/conversation.py`
- `app/main.py`
- `docs/DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md`

**Work**

1. Log the Ollama metadata for each request.
2. Compare `eval_count` with the configured `num_predict=500`\.
3. Inspect `done_reason`\.
4. Inspect the actual response in browser developer tools.
5. Compare the same prompt through the direct Ollama CLI and the FastAPI application.
6. Test long responses with short and long conversation histories.

**How to interpret the results**

| Observation | Likely explanation |
|--------|--------|
| `eval_count` reaches 500 and response ends abruptly | Output token cap |
| `done_reason` indicates length termination | Generation limit reached |
| `done_reason` indicates normal stop well below cap | Model EOS or stop condition |
| Long history causes unusually short output | Context budget pressure |
| Network response is complete but UI is incomplete | Frontend rendering issue |
| CLI and API differ | Request configuration or prompt difference |

Do not immediately increase `num_predict` or `num_ctx`\. First establish the cause. If the output cap is responsible, increase it moderately and test the context budget before increasing the context window.

**Acceptance criterion\:** ten varied responses, including long explanatory answers, finish coherently without unexplained truncation.

### Milestone 1: Microphone capture and independent transcription

(P0 — First voice milestone)

This milestone must work without Ollama.

**Files likely to change**

```text
frontend/
├── index.html
├── app.js
└── style.css

app/
├── main.py
├── config.py
└── speech.py
```

Add the external STT executable and model under a tools/models directory, rather than mixing them into application source code.

**Work**

1. Add a microphone control.
2. Use `getUserMedia()` to obtain microphone access.
3. Use `MediaRecorder` to capture one utterance.
4. Stop and release the microphone.
5. Upload the recording to a new `/api/transcribe` endpoint.
6. Convert the recording to 16 kHz mono PCM WAV.
7. Call `whisper-cli.exe`\.
8. Return the transcript to the frontend.

**Test**

Record a short known sentence, such as\:

> My name is Jeff, and I am studying Geomatic Engineering at KNUST.

Compare the recognised text with what was actually said.

**Expected observation**

Athena displays a transcript without invoking the language model.

**Acceptance criterion**

- Microphone permission works.
- Recording starts and stops correctly.
- Audio reaches the local server.
- Transcription completes offline after model installation.
- The transcript is displayed.
- Temporary audio is removed after processing.

### Milestone 2: Connect transcription to Athena

(P0)

**Files likely to change**

- `frontend/app.js`
- `frontend/index.html`

The existing `/api/chat` endpoint can remain the intelligence interface.

**Work**

1. Display the transcript in an editable field.
2. Allow the user to correct errors.
3. Submit the confirmed text to `/api/chat`\.
4. Preserve the existing `conversation_id`\.
5. Display Athena's response normally.

**Test**

Speak a question, edit one word in the transcript, submit it, and verify that Athena responds to the corrected version.

**Acceptance criterion**

A spoken question produces a valid multi-turn response and the text chat still works independently.

### Milestone 3: Give Athena a voice

(P0)

**Files likely to change**

- `frontend/index.html`
- `frontend/app.js`
- `frontend/style.css`

**Work**

1. Retrieve available system voices using `speechSynthesis.getVoices()`\.
2. Select an English voice available on the laptop.
3. Speak the completed assistant response.
4. Add a Stop Speaking control.
5. Cancel queued speech when the user presses Stop.
6. Return to Idle when playback ends.

The browser API supports voice retrieval and queue cancellation.  [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechSynthesis?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Test**

Ask Athena a question that produces a paragraph-length response.

Verify\:

- The text appears.
- Speech starts.
- The speech can be stopped immediately.
- Starting another turn does not produce overlapping audio.

**Acceptance criterion**

Athena can complete a full spoken exchange with no manual audio-file handling by the user.

### Milestone 4: Improve speech latency

(P1 — After the first working loop)

Only pursue this after measuring the simple pipeline.

Potential improvements\:

- Split long responses at sentence boundaries.
- Queue short speech segments.
- Test Piper as the TTS provider.
- Introduce Ollama streaming.
- Start speech generation when a complete sentence becomes available.

Ollama's chat API supports streaming, and Piper's C++ API can return audio chunks.  [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/libpiper/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

However, simultaneous LLM generation and TTS synthesis could compete for CPU and memory. We should compare that against the sequential implementation.

**Acceptance criterion\:** the measured time to first audio improves without introducing dropped speech, overlapping playback, or memory pressure.

### Milestone 5: Interruption and natural turn-taking

(P2 — Only after the simple loop works)

Start with a manual interruption control\:

1. User clicks Interrupt.
2. Current speech is cancelled.
3. Microphone recording begins.
4. User speaks.
5. Athena transcribes and responds.

Later, consider\:

- Voice activity detection.
- Automatic end-of-utterance detection.
- Silence thresholds.
- Acoustic echo cancellation.
- Continuous listening as an explicit, opt-in mode.

`whisper.cpp` also provides VAD-related functionality, including configurable speech and silence thresholds.  [GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Acceptance criterion\:** the user can interrupt a response deliberately and Athena correctly processes the new utterance without confusing it with the assistant's own speech.

## 9. Minimal API changes

We should not replace the existing chat endpoint.

### Add

`POST /api/transcribe`

Input\:

- Audio file.
- Recording MIME type.
- Optional conversation identifier.

Output\:

```json
{
  "transcript": "Explain the difference between a geodetic datum and a coordinate reference system.",
  "provider": "whisper.cpp",
  "duration_ms": 0
}
```

The duration is a measured field, not a value to hardcode.

### Keep

`POST /api/chat`

This remains the text-generation endpoint.

### Later, if Piper is adopted

`POST /api/tts`

Input\:

```json
{
  "text": "Hello. What would you like to explore?"
}
```

Output: audio, preferably WAV initially.

### Later, for streaming

`POST /api/chat/stream`

This could return server-sent events containing\:

- Response text deltas.
- Completion metadata.
- Error events.

The frontend would buffer complete sentences before passing them to TTS.

**Important\:** do not add all these endpoints now. Only `/api/transcribe` is necessary for the first speech milestone. The TTS endpoint is unnecessary while browser speechSynthesis is being used.

## 10. Supporting text-engine improvements

These are worth fixing, but they should not displace voice development.

| Issue | Priority | Recommendation |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Possible response truncation | P0 | Instrument Ollama metadata first |
| Health check does not verify configured model | P1 | Compare configured model against `/api/tags` |
| Synchronous SQLite calls inside async handlers | P1 | Move DB operations to a worker thread or async DB layer if concurrency becomes meaningful |
| User message saved only after successful generation | P1 | Persist the user turn before generation; record failures separately |
| Arbitrary conversation IDs | P1 | Validate IDs as UUIDs |
| Whitespace-only messages can pass initial validation | P1 | Validate after stripping whitespace |
| Request timeout and errors | P1 | Expose clear failure states in the UI |
| No retry idempotency | P2 | Add request IDs if retries or streaming reconnection become necessary |
| No streaming | P2 | Introduce only when voice latency justifies it |

A few details matter\:

**Health endpoint\:** it currently checks whether Ollama responds to `/api/tags`, but that does not prove that `athena-llama:3b` is installed. The response should distinguish an available Ollama server from an available configured model.

**Persistence\:** the current implementation saves both user and assistant messages only after successful model generation. If Ollama fails, the user's turn is lost from the stored history. Save the user message before generation and record the response when it succeeds.

**SQLite\:** the current database is small, so the synchronous calls are not necessarily a serious problem in a single-user prototype. They do block the async event loop, though, and should be addressed before multiple simultaneous operations become common.

**Streaming\:** the current `stream=False` behaviour is reasonable for debugging and the first voice loop. Ollama's API defaults to streaming when the parameter is omitted, so changing to streaming later requires explicit handling of the incremental response format.  [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

I would not introduce vector databases, complex memory systems, multiple agents, Docker, or background services at this stage.

## 11. Performance and benchmark plan

We need real measurements from the Ryzen laptop. The published benchmarks are useful for choosing candidates, but they cannot tell us exactly how Athena will behave.

### Measurements to collect

| Stage | Measurement | Why it matters |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Idle system | Available RAM and committed memory | Establish baseline |
| Ollama | Load time, generation time, token counts | Measure intelligence latency |
| STT | Transcription time and peak memory | Determine whether Whisper is practical |
| TTS | Synthesis time and generated audio duration | Determine whether speech keeps pace |
| Full voice loop | End-of-recording to first audio | Actual conversational responsiveness |
| Full turn | End-to-end completion time | User experience |

### Benchmark procedure

Use the same recordings for every STT candidate\:

- 5-second clip.
- 15-second clip.
- 30-second clip.
- A longer conversational clip.

Run cold and warm tests where applicable. Repeat each test ten times if practical and report median and worst-case values.

For STT, calculate\:

$$
RTF = \frac{\text{transcription time}}{\text{recording duration}}
$$

An RTF below 1 means transcription is faster than the duration of the recording.

A proposed target is RTF at or below 1 for ordinary push-to-talk speech, with up to 1.5 as a tolerable early-prototype result.

For TTS\:

$$
RTF_{TTS} =
\frac{\text{synthesis time}}{\text{generated audio duration}}
$$

For the full system\:

$$
TTFA =
t_{\text{first audio}} - t_{\text{recording ended}}
$$

That last metric is particularly important. It measures how long the user waits after finishing a question before hearing Athena speak.

We should also record\:

- CPU utilisation.
- Peak RAM.
- Whether Windows begins paging heavily.
- Ollama model reload time.
- Whether speech output stutters.
- Whether the system becomes unresponsive.

The acceptance criteria should be based on actual usability, not a fabricated benchmark number.

## 12. Ghanaian English and Twi evaluation

This needs deliberate testing. We should not assume that an English model will automatically recognise every Ghanaian accent accurately.

### Ghanaian English

Whisper is multilingual and trained on diverse speech, but the reviewed official material does not establish a Ghanaian-English accuracy benchmark for this laptop or microphone.  [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/whisper?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

We should create a small evaluation set of our own.

Suggested test vocabulary\:

- KNUST
- Kumasi
- Ayeduase
- Obuasi
- Geomatics
- Geodetic datum
- Coordinate reference system
- GNSS
- Cadastral
- WGS84
- UTM Zone 30N
- Land registration

Test\:

1. Clear English.
2. Natural conversational Ghanaian English.
3. Faster speech.
4. Sentences with technical vocabulary.
5. Names and numbers.
6. Sentences with occasional code-switching.

Compare the transcript against a manually prepared reference.

Use word error rate\:

$$
WER = \frac{S + D + I}{N}
$$

Where\:

- $S$ \= substitutions.
- $D$ \= deletions.
- $I$ \= insertions.
- $N$ \= words in the reference transcript.

A transcript that sounds plausible but changes a technical term is a failure, even if the overall WER is reasonable.

### Twi

The reviewed candidates do not provide a dependable plug-and-play Twi voice pipeline\:

| System | Twi support in reviewed documentation |
|--------|--------|
| Whisper | Twi is absent from its published language-token list |
| Vosk | Twi is not in its published language/model list |
| Piper | No Twi voice listed |
| Kokoro | No Twi language pipeline listed |

 [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/tokenizer.py?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [alphacephei.com](https://alphacephei.com/vosk/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl/blob/main/docs/VOICES.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [GitHub](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This does not prove that no research model or community implementation exists. It means we should not promise Twi support using these particular candidates.

For now, evaluate English first, then test code-switching. A proper Twi feature may eventually require a different model or a specifically trained voice.

## 13. Risks and controls

| Risk | Control |
|--------|--------|
| Speech service sends audio externally | Use local Whisper for default STT |
| Recognition changes technical meaning | Show editable transcript before submission |
| Large models exhaust RAM | Start with base.en and sequential inference |
| Assistant hears itself | Stop microphone while speaking |
| Recording remains on disk | Use temporary files and delete them |
| Microphone permission denied | Show a clear permission error |
| Browser codec differs | Inspect supported MIME types |
| Piper voice has restrictive licence | Read the actual voice model card and training lineage |
| Speech is too slow | Measure RTF and TTFA before optimising |
| User is interrupted by long responses | Add Stop Speaking in the first TTS milestone |

There is one design principle I would preserve throughout: **Athena should never silently activate the microphone or record continuously in this first version.** Voice input should be deliberate and visible.

## 15. Prioritised development plan

## Athena Voice v0.1

Proposed development order

1. **P0 — Stabilise the text endpoint**
   
   Verify the truncation cause and capture Ollama metadata.
2. **P0 — Build independent speech recognition**
   
   Browser microphone → local Whisper → visible transcript.
3. **P0 — Connect speech to the existing conversation**
   
   Confirm transcript → Ollama → displayed response.
4. **P0 — Make Athena speak**
   
   Browser TTS, voice selection, stop control.
5. **P1 — Improve responsiveness**
   
   Benchmark, test Piper, then consider chunked output and streaming.
6. **P2 — Natural interruption**
   
   Manual barge-in first, VAD and more advanced turn-taking later.

## What we should build first

**The first real deliverable should be a working push-to-talk loop using local Whisper and the existing Ollama model.**

I would not begin by installing Piper, Kokoro, faster-whisper, Vosk, and several other speech packages. That would create unnecessary variables and consume time before we have a working baseline.

The first practical session should do three things\:

1. Instrument the current text endpoint.
2. Verify `whisper.cpp` can transcribe a known WAV file on the laptop.
3. Add the microphone button and `/api/transcribe` endpoint.

Once that works, connect it to the existing chat route. Then make Athena speak.

That gives us a complete, testable voice assistant before we attempt more advanced conversational behaviour.

**The larger product vision remains intact\:** identity, continuity, intelligence, agency and presence. But presence begins with reliable turn-taking, not a flashy animated orb. Athena must hear correctly, understand the conversation, respond usefully, and speak naturally. Everything else can evolve from that foundation.
